title: Test 1: Foundations of Physical Geography
sub: Units 1–4 · pages 7–65  ·  50 points  ·  50 minutes  ·  Closed book
instructions: Read each question carefully. Circle one answer for multiple choice. Write on the lines provided; use the back of the page if you need more room. Point values are shown for each section.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly lists the components of Earth that physical geography studies?
choices: Lithosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere, atmosphere, and interior
questions.why: p. 8 — the opening definition of the discipline.

questions.stem: In a well-designed experiment, the one factor that the scientist deliberately manipulates is the
questions.why: p. 12 — everything else must be held constant; those are the experimental controls. What changes as a result is the dependent variable.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a great circle?
questions.why: p. 14 — the Equator is the only parallel that is a great circle. All other parallels, including both tropics and both polar circles, are small circles.

questions.stem: The observation that light from essentially every distant galaxy is redshifted supports the conclusion that
choices: all galaxies formed at the same time
the Milky Way sits at the center of the universe
questions.why: p. 24 — if every galaxy is moving away from every other galaxy, space itself must be expanding.

questions.stem: A galaxy that is egg-shaped, reddish to yellowish, and made up mostly of old stars with very little gas and dust is
questions.why: p. 30 — the color is the clue. Reddish and yellowish means old stars; blue means young stars still forming from gas and dust.

questions.stem: Elements heavier than iron are created
choices: in the first few minutes after the Big Bang
in the cores of ordinary main-sequence stars
questions.why: p. 37 — fusing elements heavier than iron consumes more energy than it produces, so ordinary stars stop at iron. A supernova carries enough energy to make gold, silver, and uranium.

questions.stem: Which sequence lists the eons of geologic time from oldest to youngest?
questions.why: p. 45 — the first three together account for almost 90% of Earth’s history.

questions.stem: A geologist finds a sandstone layer lying beneath a shale layer in an undisturbed sequence. Which principle tells her the sandstone is older?
questions.why: p. 47 — in an undisturbed sequence, the layers on the bottom are the oldest.

questions.stem: A mineral sample has a daughter-to-parent ratio of 1. How many half-lives have passed?
questions.why: p. 49 — a ratio of 1 means 50% parent and 50% daughter, which is exactly one half-life. A ratio of 3 (25% parent, 75% daughter) would be two half-lives.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the largest-scale map?
questions.why: p. 53 — the smaller the denominator, the larger the scale, and the more detail is shown. A campus map is large-scale; a world map is small-scale.

questions.stem: A cartographer is making a world map so that readers can compare how much cropland each country has in production. The best choice is
choices: a conformal projection such as Mercator
an equal-area projection such as Gall-Peters
any projection, since all of them preserve area
questions.why: p. 61 — the reader is comparing quantities spread over areas, so relative area must be true even if shapes are distorted.

questions.stem: On a topographic map drawn with a 20-foot contour interval, labeled index contours would appear every
questions.why: p. 55 — every fifth contour line is an index contour, and 5 × 20 ft = 100 ft. Index contours are the only ones labeled.

questions.stem: Write the letter of the correct definition next to each term.
right: The study of layered sedimentary rocks
Using the geometry of triangles to determine a location
The study, practice, and interpretation of maps
Fossil assemblages are unique to the time in which they lived
Reducing the complexity of the characteristics being mapped
Giving non-spatial data a geographic location
“The present is the key to the past”
questions.why: 1 point each. Cartography p. 52 · Cosmology p. 23 · Stratigraphy p. 47 · Geocoding p. 18 · Uniformitarianism p. 47 · Fossil succession p. 47 · Triangulation p. 19 · Generalization p. 52.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between relative dating and absolute dating, and name the scientific discovery that made absolute dating possible.
questions.answer: Relative dating establishes only the order of events — whether one rock is older or younger than another. Absolute dating assigns a numerical age in years. The discovery of radioactivity in the late 1800s made it possible.
questions.rubric: 1 pt relative = order without numbers; 1 pt absolute = specific numerical age; 1 pt radioactivity (accept “radio-isotopic dating” or “isotopic dating techniques” developed in the early 20th century). (pp. 47–48)

questions.stem: Why is the Equator the only parallel that is also a great circle?
questions.answer: Because a great circle must divide the Earth into two equal halves, and the Equator is the only line of latitude that does so.
questions.rubric: 2 pts for the definition of a great circle — any circle that divides the Earth into two equal halves, and the largest circle that can be drawn on a sphere. 1 pt for recognizing that every other parallel is smaller and cuts the Earth unevenly, making it a small circle. (p. 14)

questions.stem: Name the three geospatial technologies covered in Unit 1, and give one thing each is used for.
questions.answer: Remote sensing, global positioning systems (GPS), and geographic information systems (GIS).
questions.rubric: 1 pt each, requiring both the name and a defensible use. Remote sensing — studying objects without physical contact, via satellite imagery, aerial photography, radar, or lidar. GPS — determining an accurate location on Earth’s surface using at least four satellites and triangulation. GIS — bringing spatial and non-spatial data together in layers for storage and analysis. (pp. 18–21)

questions.stem: A star like our Sun and a star many times more massive both eventually run out of fuel. Describe how their final states differ.
questions.answer: A Sun-like star stops fusion and collapses into a white dwarf. A much more massive star explodes as a supernova, leaving behind either a neutron star or a black hole.
questions.rubric: 1.5 pts for the Sun-like path — red giant, then fusion stops, then gravitational collapse to a white dwarf about the size of Earth, which fades out. 1.5 pts for the massive path — red supergiant, fusion continues up to iron, then core collapse produces a supernova, leaving a neutron star (core under about four solar masses) or a black hole (core over about five solar masses). (pp. 36–38)

questions.stem: Every flat map of the world is wrong in some way. Explain why this is unavoidable, name the three map properties a cartographer must choose among, and explain how a cartographer decides which one to preserve. Support your answer with at least two specific named projections.
questions.rubric:
2 pts — why distortion is unavoidable. A globe is three-dimensional and a map is two-dimensional, so flattening always requires shearing, tearing, or compression. The orange-peel analogy earns full credit here. Since no projection can preserve every property, some distortion is guaranteed.

2 pts — the three properties. Shape, area, and distance. (Accept “shape and angle” for the first.)

2 pts — how the choice is made, with two named projections. The cartographer decides which property matters most for the map’s purpose. Expect examples such as: Mercator (conformal — correct shapes and angles, badly distorted area; good for navigation, topography, weather); Gall-Peters (equal-area — true relative sizes, distorted shapes; good for density and thematic maps); Azimuthal Equidistant (correct distance and direction from a center point; good for flight paths or earthquake epicenters); Robinson (a compromise that minimizes all distortion rather than eliminating any; good for general-purpose world maps); Goode Homolosine (interrupted — accepts tearing to preserve area).

Award full credit for any two correctly described projections tied to a purpose. (pp. 57–63)
